Bernard André, O.E.S.A. (1450–1522), also known as Andreas, was a French Augustinian friar, poet, chronicler of the reign of Henry VII of England, and poet laureate. He was appointed as a tutor to Henry VII's son, Arthur, Prince of Wales, and later wrote a chronicle of the prince's life and reign. André was also a prolific poet, writing in both French and Latin, and his works include sonnets, ballads, and hymns. His poetry often explored themes of love, faith, and mortality, and he was particularly known for his use of symbolism and imagery. André's contributions to the field of historical writing and poetry are still studied and admired today, and he is remembered as one of the most important figures in the development of French literature during the Renaissance.

André's work also had a significant impact on the cultural and intellectual landscape of Europe during the 16th century. His writings on the life and reign of Henry VII helped to shape the way historians understood the English monarchy, while his poetry influenced the development of the Renaissance humanist movement. Furthermore, André's use of symbolism and imagery in his poetry helped to pave the way for later literary movements, such as Symbolism and Surrealism.

Despite his significant contributions to literature and history, André's life and work have often been overlooked in favor of more prominent figures of the Renaissance. However, his impact on the development of French literature and his influence on later literary movements make him a fascinating and important figure in the history of literature.

The legacy of Bernard André can be seen in the many writers and artists who were influenced by his work. His poetry and historical writings continue to be studied and admired today, and his influence can be seen in the works of writers such as François Rabelais and Pierre de Ronsard.
